design_detail: Cross-sectional survey (STROBE) in 2553 young adults, the 2018 to 2019 wave (June 2018 to October 2019, one year after high-school graduation) of the Happiness and Health Study, a cohort first recruited in Southern California high schools. Self-reported nicotine vaping and cannabis vaping, each in five levels of recency and frequency, against three self-reported respiratory outcomes (bronchitic symptoms, wheeze, shortness of breath), analysed by logistic regression with sociodemographic adjustment and then with full adjustment for the other vaping, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. The cannabis vaping variable combines electronic devices for THC or hash oil with vaping concentrated cannabis (dabs).
can_establish: In one regional cohort of young adults surveyed in 2018 to 2019, whether people who reported vaping THC or hash oil (or dabs) also reported more bronchitic symptoms, wheeze or shortness of breath than people who reported never doing so, and whether that survived adjustment for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis.
cannot_establish: Which came first, vaping or the symptoms (one time point); what product, device, additive or amount was vaped (none recorded); lung function (symptoms were self-reported, with no spirometry); whether the link is the same for older adults, other regions or people not in school; absolute risk in each vaping group (Table 2 gives shares of cases, not symptom rates by group); and whether residual confounding by other exposures, such as tobacco in joints or blunts, accounts for it.

sample.recruitment: Participants of the Happiness and Health Study, originally recruited from high schools throughout Southern California and surveyed in this wave one year after graduation (June 2018 to October 2019); 2553 provided vaping data (75% participation rate). Of these, 2389 (94%) had complete data on shortness of breath, 2396 (94%) on wheeze and 2194 (86%) on chronic bronchitis (Methods › Analytic Sample).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Provision of data on lifetime, past 6-month and past 30-day vaping. People who gave no respiratory data stay in the vaping sample but drop out of the outcome models.
sample.demographics: Mean age 19.3 years (SD 0.79); 1477 women (57.9%) and 1076 men; 1188 Hispanic (47.3%), 454 non-Hispanic Asian (18.1%), 413 non-Hispanic white (16.5%), 166 multiracial (6.6%), 120 Black (4.8%), 109 Pacific Islander (4.3%), 60 other (2.4%), 43 not given; mean body mass index 24.97 (SD 6.51); 1081 of 2392 who answered (45.2%) lived comfortably; 161 gave no financial status (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 75% of the original sample took part in this wave. Per the Methods, people without any respiratory data were less likely to report never having vaped nicotine or smoked cigarettes (eTable 1, in the Supplement, not opened). Outcome data were missing for 359 people (bronchitic symptoms), 157 (wheeze) and 164 (shortness of breath); 110 had no cannabis vaping data and 2 no nicotine vaping data (Table 2 footnotes).
sample.selection_effects: A school-based Southern California cohort that is not nationally representative, ethnically diverse, all aged about 19, a year after leaving high school; the authors say findings may not apply to other regions or to people who did not attend or finish high school. Those who did not take part, or gave no respiratory data, differed in vaping and smoking, so a selected group may be analysed.

exposure.measurement: Self-report questionnaire. For each substance, people answered whether they had ever used it, and whether in the last 6 months; those with use in the last 6 months gave days of use in the past month. Items covered e-cigarettes with nicotine, JUUL or similar, other electronic vaping devices, an electronic device to vape THC or hash oil or dabs (wax, shatter, budder, butane hash oil), cigarettes, smoking marijuana, and blunts. Two five-level variables were built (nicotine vaping; cannabis vaping): never; lifetime but not in the past 6 months; past 6 months but not the past 30 days; 1 or 2 days in the past 30; 3 or more days in the past 30. Combustible cannabis (marijuana cigarettes, joints, blunts) and cigarettes were coded the same way (Methods › Measures).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recency and days of use in the past month only. No information on the product (cartridge, dry-herb, concentrate), device, source, additives, amounts per session, puffing or time since first use. The cannabis vaping variable lumps vaping THC or hash oil in electronic devices with vaping concentrated cannabis (dabs), so cartridge use and dabbing cannot be separated.
exposure.polysubstance: Large overlap between nicotine vaping, cigarettes, smoked cannabis and cannabis vaping (eTable 2, in the Supplement, not opened). The full model adjusts for the other three exposures at five levels each, so the cannabis vaping estimates are mutually adjusted for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. Combustible cannabis includes blunts; whether tobacco was involved in joints or blunts is not recorded. Alcohol, other drugs and secondhand smoke exposure are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (survey). Exposure categories are by recency, not verified by biomarker.

comparison.controls: Young adults who reported never vaping cannabis (1504 of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data, 61.6%). This group includes people who smoked cannabis or cigarettes or vaped nicotine; those exposures are adjusted for in the full model, not excluded. For nicotine vaping the comparison group is people who reported never vaping nicotine (1456 of 2553).
comparison.matching: None. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, personal financial status and body mass index (sociodemographic model); the full model adds the other vaping variable, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use, each in five levels.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Asthma and allergy history (the authors used wheeze rather than a diagnosis because most asthma starts early), secondhand smoke, air quality including wildfire smoke, housing, respiratory infections, mental health and symptom-reporting style, other inhaled substances, and any symptom that came before the first vaping. Not measured or not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Reference group contains people who used the other substances; handled by statistical adjustment with coarse five-level frequency bands (the top band is 3 or more days in the past 30, which hides daily use).

outcomes.instruments: Three self-reported outcomes, each analysed separately. Bronchitic symptoms: any of daily morning cough for 3 months in a row, daily cough at other times of day for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm other than with a cold, and bronchitis in the past 12 months. Wheeze or whistling in the chest in the past 12 months (yes or no). Shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill (yes or no). The authors base the definitions on earlier reports (references 6 and 9: a 2019 review by Gotts and colleagues and a 2017 adolescent cohort study by McConnell and colleagues; not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: No spirometry or clinical examination; symptoms are self-reported by people who also self-reported their vaping. Whether the 12-month window applies to all four bronchitic items is unclear: the abstract states it for the composite, the Methods only for the bronchitis item. Shortness of breath has no time frame.
outcomes.operationalization: Having the outcome means answering yes to any bronchitic item, or yes to wheeze, or yes to breathlessness; no symptom severity, duration of vaping before symptoms or clinical diagnosis.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The Methods state that Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values were used to correct for multiple tests, but no adjusted P value appears in the Results or Table 3; the printed intervals are unadjusted. There are 48 odds ratios in Table 3 (3 outcomes, 2 exposures, 4 levels, 2 models), several with a lower bound close to 1 (1.01, 1.02, 1.04).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed survey). Exposure and outcome were reported by the same person at the same time, which allows correlated reporting.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) against never, for lifetime but not past 6 months, past 6 months but not past 30 days, 1 to 2 days in the past 30, and 3 or more days in the past 30 (sociodemographic model; full model). CANNABIS VAPING, bronchitic symptoms: sociodemographic 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84); full 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96), 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56), 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47), 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: sociodemographic 1.06 (0.65 to 1.73), 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00), 1.76 (0.96 to 3.13), 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36); full 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: sociodemographic 0.95 (0.63 to 1.44), 1.35 (1.04 to 1.75), 1.67 (0.98 to 2.86), 1.67 (1.09 to 2.53); full 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). NICOTINE VAPING, bronchitic symptoms: sociodemographic 1.35 (0.92 to 1.97), 1.18 (0.79 to 1.78), 1.48 (0.97 to 2.21), 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41); full 1.21 (0.76 to 1.93), 0.82 (0.50 to 1.32), 1.13 (0.71 to 1.81), 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46). Wheeze: sociodemographic 1.13 (0.74 to 1.71), 1.55 (1.04 to 2.32), 1.27 (0.81 to 1.99), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96); full 0.96 (0.58 to 1.59), 1.06 (0.66 to 1.71), 0.99 (0.59 to 1.65), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35). Shortness of breath: sociodemographic 1.20 (0.85 to 1.71), 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), 1.64 (1.14 to 2.36), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full 1.03 (0.68 to 1.57), 1.10 (0.73 to 1.67), 1.31 (0.86 to 1.99), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Overall 17.5% (384 of 2194) reported bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2396) wheeze and 20.4% (488 of 2389) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis, against 61.6% of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data (Table 2 and Results). Editors' rough calculation, not in the paper: if people with missing outcome data were spread evenly across vaping groups, unadjusted bronchitic-symptom rates would be about 14% in people who never vaped cannabis and about 27% to 31% in those who vaped it in the past 30 days; the paper says missing respiratory data were commoner in people who vaped nicotine or smoked, so the true gap may be larger. Odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common (13% to 20%).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, personal financial status, body mass index; the full model adds the other vaping variable, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. No adjustment for asthma, secondhand smoke, air quality or tobacco co-use in cannabis. The number of people in each model is not given: Table 3 headings show 2194, 2396 and 2389, the counts with outcome data, but the full models also need cannabis vaping, financial status and body mass index.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All three outcomes and both exposures are shown in Table 3, with sociodemographic and full models. The abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3 and the Results text (reporting issue 1). The stated multiple-testing correction is not shown. The headline emphasises the cannabis vaping results in the full model; the nicotine vaping associations seen in the sociodemographic model, which became null on full adjustment, are reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The nicotine and cannabis vaping top bands are small (400 and 155 people), and the cannabis vaping intervals at 1 to 2 and 3 or more days are wide (1.42 to 5.47; 1.18 to 4.06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 2553 young adults in one Southern California school-based cohort, people who reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs had higher odds than people who never had of reporting bronchitic symptoms in the past year at every level of recency and frequency (full-model adjusted odds ratios 1.6 to 2.8, adjusting for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis), higher odds of wheeze only in the top band (3 or more days in the past 30, 2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and no reliable difference in shortness of breath. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with bronchitic symptoms, wheeze and shortness of breath after sociodemographic adjustment only (1.45 to 1.78), and with none of them after full adjustment (0.85 to 0.96).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say cannabis vaping is associated with increased risk of bronchitic symptoms and wheeze, independent of nicotine vaping and smoking combustible products, and that nicotine and cannabis vaping warrant consideration in patient care and public health policy. Key Points say cannabis vaping may be associated with bronchitic symptoms beyond the consequences of other drug use. Gaps: (1) risk language comes from one cross-sectional survey, with no information on what came first; (2) independence rests on adjustment with coarse five-level bands for the other exposures, and combustible cannabis includes blunts with unrecorded tobacco, so residual confounding is plausible; (3) odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people who had last vaped cannabis more than 6 months earlier (1.73), about as raised as in those vaping in the past 30 days (2.19 to 2.79), which does not fit an effect of recent vaping alone and is not discussed; (4) the Discussion's mechanisms (vitamin E acetate, higher exposure from deeper puffs and concentrates) were not measured, and the statement that vitamin E acetate vaping has virtually disappeared is made without a source; (5) the abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3; (6) symptoms are self-reported and unconfirmed. The Limitations section does state the cross-sectional design, the single region and the need for longitudinal work.

timeline.event: McConnell et al. (cited, not read) linked nicotine vaping to respiratory symptoms in adolescents; Wills et al. (2019) did the same in adults, per the authors' introduction (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

This survey, which the authors describe as new evidence for an independent association of cannabis vaping with bronchitic symptoms, with nicotine vaping and smoking adjusted at the same time; they note longitudinal work on cannabis vaping and symptoms is lacking (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Limitations).

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional survey from one cohort. No second study of cannabis vaping and respiratory symptoms was read for this card, and the authors say longitudinal research on this question is lacking. Evidence on smoked cannabis and symptoms, cited by the authors, is not read here.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health: grants U54CA180905 (all authors; principal investigator Leventhal), R01CA229617-01 (Barrington-Trimis, Leventhal) and K24DA048160 (Leventhal). The paper states the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young adults with repeated symptom reports and lung function tests before and after people start vaping cannabis, recording product type (cartridge, dry-herb, concentrate), source, device and puffing, tobacco co-use, and biomarker confirmation of use, with separate groups who only vape cannabis, only smoke it, do both, or neither, and a registered analysis plan with the multiple-testing correction shown.

domains.note: One time point, so reverse causation and shared causes cannot be separated. Adjustment is for sociodemographics and for the other exposures in five coarse bands; tobacco in joints or blunts, secondhand smoke, air quality, asthma and allergy are not measured. Raised odds in people who last vaped cannabis more than 6 months before the survey (1.73) point to residual confounding or to an exposure measure that captures more than recent vaping.

Self-reported recency and days of use, not verified; the cannabis vaping variable merges THC or hash oil devices with dabs, and no product, device or amount is recorded. Misclassification is probably not related to symptoms, which would bias towards no association.

A school-based Southern California cohort, 75% participation in this wave; people without respiratory data were more likely to have vaped nicotine or smoked cigarettes; not representative of other regions or of people who left school.
Not an issue for a single-time survey of exposure and symptoms.

Outcome data missing for 14% (bronchitic symptoms) and 6% (wheeze, shortness of breath), with missingness related to vaping and smoking; 110 people have no cannabis vaping data; handling is not described and the number analysed in each model is not given.

Self-reported symptoms from questions used in earlier cohort studies, with no spirometry or clinician; the bronchitic composite counts any of four broad items; the same person reported exposure and outcome.

No protocol or registration; the stated Benjamini-Hochberg correction is not shown; the abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3; all outcomes and both models are shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain; confounding is judged high because a single cross-sectional survey with coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures and from reverse causation, and the pattern of raised odds in people who last vaped long before the survey suggests residual confounding. The study is sizeable for a vaping survey, adjusts at once for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis, reports both an unadjusted-to-sociodemographic and a fully adjusted model, and shows its null results. It may be cited for the association between self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil or dabs and self-reported bronchitic symptoms (and, in the top band, wheeze) in these young adults, and for the loss of the nicotine vaping association on full adjustment. It may not be cited for causation, for the effect of any particular product, for lung function, for absolute risk in a vaping group, or for older people.

key_findings.finding: 2553 young adults (mean age 19.3, SD 0.79; 57.9% women; 47.3% Hispanic) from a Southern California school-based cohort answered a survey between June 2018 and October 2019, a year after high-school graduation (75% participation). Outcome data were available for 2194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2396 (wheeze) and 2389 (shortness of breath).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Analytic Sample, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Of the 2553, 1095 (42.9%) reported ever vaping nicotine. Of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data, 939 (38.4%) reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs: 204 (8.4%) only in their lifetime, 490 (20.1%) in the past 6 months but not the past 30 days, 90 (3.7%) on 1 or 2 days and 155 (6.3%) on 3 or more days in the past 30; 110 people had no cannabis vaping data. Smoked cannabis on 3 or more days in the past 30: 517 (20.3%); cigarettes on 3 or more days: 98 (3.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2 footnote f

key_findings.finding: Overall, 384 of 2194 (17.5%) reported bronchitic symptoms, 312 of 2396 (13.0%) wheeze in the past year, and 488 of 2389 (20.4%) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis. Table 2's percentages are shares of people with each outcome, not rates within each vaping group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 2's heading calls these prevalence, but footnote a says column percentages.

key_findings.finding: Bronchitic symptoms and cannabis vaping, full model (adjusted for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking, smoked cannabis, age, sex, race/ethnicity, financial status, body mass index), adjusted odds ratios against never vaping cannabis: lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Sociodemographic model only: 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (bronchitic symptoms columns, frequency of vaping cannabis rows); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract prints 1.83 (1.08 to 3.10), 1.58 (1.02 to 2.46), 2.83 (1.46 to 5.50) and 2.14 (1.16 to 3.92) for the same four; use Table 3.

key_findings.finding: Wheeze and cannabis vaping, full model: 3 or more days in the past 30 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37); other levels not reliably raised (1.12, 1.47, 1.84; intervals include 1). Sociodemographic model: 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36) in the top band and 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00) for past 6 months but not past 30 days.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (wheeze columns); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Shortness of breath and cannabis vaping: sociodemographic model raised at 3 or more days (1.67, 1.09 to 2.53) and past 6 months only (1.35, 1.04 to 1.75); in the full model no level was reliably raised (0.90 to 1.55; 3 or more days 1.41, 0.80 to 2.48).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (shortness of breath columns); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, sociodemographic model: bronchitic symptoms 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), wheeze 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), shortness of breath 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96). Full model: 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42); no nicotine vaping level was reliably associated with any outcome. The authors say residual confounding by cannabis vaping and by smoking cigarettes or cannabis could partly explain the earlier associations.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (frequency of vaping nicotine rows); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The Results sentence on nicotine and bronchitic symptoms gives the cannabis ranges (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Limits and explanations given by the authors: cross-sectional design (temporality unknown); school-based Southern California sample with 75% participation, not nationally representative; the cannabis vaping measure includes dabs; longitudinal research on cannabis vaping and symptoms lacking; possible reasons for a difference from nicotine vaping include the chemicals in THC e-liquids, device and heating differences, tampering with products, and deeper or longer puffs. None of these was measured.
Funding: National Cancer Institute grants U54CA180905, R01CA229617-01 and K24DA048160; funders had no role; no conflicts reported.
key_findings.locator: Article notes (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's fully adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms with cannabis vaping (1.83, 1.08 to 3.10; 1.58, 1.02 to 2.46; 2.83, 1.46 to 5.50; 2.14, 1.16 to 3.92) differ from Table 3 and the Results text (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96; 1.63, 1.04 to 2.56; 2.79, 1.42 to 5.47; 2.19, 1.18 to 4.06). The wheeze value (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37) is the same in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract appears to quote an earlier version of the model. Table 3 is used for every figure; the direction and the conclusion are unchanged, but the abstract values must not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 204 of 2553 (8.4%) for lifetime-only cannabis vaping and 939 of 2553 (38.4%) for any, but 8.4% and 38.4% are shares of the 2443 people with cannabis vaping data (204 of 2553 is 8.0%, as in Table 2; 939 of 2553 is 36.8%). The abstract also says lifetime but not in the past '60 months'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mixed denominators and a typing error (6 months); the 110 people with no cannabis vaping data are the difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results sentence on nicotine vaping and bronchitic symptoms in the fully adjusted model gives 'aORs range from 1.63-2.79 [95% CI, 1.01-5.47]', which are the cannabis vaping figures. Table 3 gives 0.82 to 1.21 for nicotine vaping.
reporting_issues.consequence: A copy error; the table shows no reliable nicotine vaping association with bronchitic symptoms on full adjustment, consistent with the sentence's claim of no significant association.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is headed 'Prevalence of each respiratory outcome', but the percentages are column percentages (the share of people with each outcome who fell in each vaping group), not symptom rates within each vaping group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper never gives the percentage of each vaping group with symptoms; do not read the 48.2% of cases who never vaped cannabis as the rate in that group.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 headings give n = 2194, 2396 and 2389 (people with outcome data), but the fully adjusted models also need cannabis vaping (110 missing), financial status (161 missing), body mass index and the smoking variables. The Methods also say 2553 provided complete data on lifetime, 6-month and 30-day vaping while 110 have no cannabis vaping data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 headings; Methods › Analytic Sample; Table 2 footnote f
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people in each model is not stated; complete-case loss may be larger than 14%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values corrected for multiple tests; no adjusted P value or adjusted interval is shown. Several fully adjusted lower bounds are close to 1 (1.01 for lifetime-only cannabis vaping and bronchitic symptoms; 1.04 and 1.02 elsewhere).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the weaker associations survive the stated correction cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The pattern of odds in Table 3 is not discussed: people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey had raised odds of bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), similar to those vaping in the past 30 days (2.19 to 2.79).
reporting_issues.consequence: The data do not show a clear gradient with recency, which argues for caution about an effect of current vaping and for residual confounding.
